strengths: Systematic and comprehensive exploration moving beyond isolated task evaluation with multiple analysis dimensions (computational efficiency, ASR fine-tuning variants, representation analysis, SUPERB probing)

Strong empirical results in specific scenarios: linear-time scaling advantage clearly demonstrated; long-context ASR achieves 11.08% WER where Transformer fails (OOM); causal ASR achieves better accuracy with 17% fewer parameters

Rigorous analysis methodology: phone purity at multiple granularities, CCA with multiple speech attributes, statistical significance testing with paired t-tests, ablation studies on bidirectional architectures
Well-executed experimental design following established HuBERT training pipeline with transparent implementation details and reproducible setup
Clear presentation with informative visualizations (especially MACs/RTF scaling in Figure 1) and comprehensive result tables
weaknesses: Significant bidirectional underperformance: ExtBiMamba achieves 815.38 SUPERB score vs. 868.93 for Transformer at base scale (~7% degradation), with competitive performance only at smaller scales—this limits practical applicability since bidirectional models are more widely used

Unresolved representation-performance mismatch: ExtBiMamba shows higher phone purity than Transformer yet achieves worse phoneme recognition (10.65% vs 7.49% PER); authors acknowledge but only provide speculative explanations rather than investigation or resolution

Training setup concerns reducing confidence in fair comparison: single GPU with 8× larger batch size results in ~1/4 audio duration per batch vs. original HuBERT—this substantial deviation may differentially impact architectures and complicates interpretation of results
Limited novelty: straightforward application of existing Mamba to existing HuBERT pipeline without methodological innovation or new training techniques

Narrow practical applicability: main advantages restricted to causal/streaming ASR (niche use case); bidirectional setting underperforms; unclear guidance on when practitioners should adopt Mamba-based models
Incomplete scope of evaluation: ASR evaluation only on TEDLIUM3 (single dataset); SUPERB evaluation uses 4-task subset rather than full benchmark; no evaluation beyond ASR and SUPERB tasks

Insufficient analysis of bidirectional underperformance: limited investigation into *why* Mamba fails at base scale; bidirectional designs appear ad-hoc; no ablation on hyperparameters or architectural components
Incomplete statistical testing: significance testing only for long-context ASR; no statistical significance provided for SUPERB results or most downstream comparisons

Overstated claims in abstract/conclusions: 'superior performance for streaming ASR' and 'competitive SUPERB performance' downplay substantial bidirectional underperformance; insufficient delineation of applicability boundaries

strengths: Systematic multi-faceted empirical evaluation across efficiency, fine-tuning, and representation analysis
Clear quantitative evidence of Mamba's linear-time complexity advantage with MACs/RTF measurements on long sequences
Practical demonstrations of long-context ASR (13.37%→11.08% WER with statistical significance) and streaming ASR improvements
Transparent reporting of limitations and performance trade-offs without overselling results
Multiple complementary representation analysis methods (phone purity, CCA, layer-wise analysis)
weaknesses: Critical experimental setup issue: training with 1/4 audio duration per batch due to single-GPU constraints undermines fair comparison with standard HuBERT protocols; results may reflect training differences rather than architectural merit

Unresolved methodological contradiction: ExtBiMamba shows higher phone purity than Transformer yet significantly worse phoneme recognition performance (10.65% vs 7.49%), with only speculative explanations provided

Significant scalability failure in bidirectional setting not adequately addressed: base-size ExtBiMamba underperforms Transformer by ~6% on SUPERB_S, contradicting efficiency motivation; ablation shows InnBiMamba substantially better, suggesting poorly justified initial choices
Limited novelty: purely empirical evaluation of existing components with no new methods or theoretical insights; related work (Zhang et al., SSAM) already explores Mamba-based speech SSL
Narrow downstream evaluation: only 4 of 12 SUPERB tasks tested; single-domain long-context evaluation (TEDLIUM3); weak justification for MiniSUPERB subset selection
Causal setting advantages unexplained: no ablations clarify why Mamba excels in causal but fails in bidirectional settings, limiting interpretability
Reproducibility concerns: single-GPU training with non-standard batch size, no code release mentioned, InnBiMamba/ExtBiMamba implementation details incomplete

Incomplete analysis: CCA findings (speaker similarity) are descriptive without mechanistic understanding; long-context benefit claims ('consistent rare word recognition') are anecdotal and unquantified
Unfair long-context comparison: Transformer hits OOM on document-level but no utterance-level comparison to isolate architectural constraints from memory limits
Limited statistical rigor: significance testing only for one experiment; most SUPERB differences not tested despite small margins; potential stability issues from single-GPU training

strengths: Comprehensive and systematic exploration: First thorough investigation of Mamba-based HuBERT covering computational efficiency, long-context ASR, streaming ASR, SUPERB probing, representation analysis, and ablation studies

Clear practical advantages with concrete evidence: Linear scaling vs. quadratic (Figure 1), long-context ASR where Transformer OOMs (11.08% WER vs. OOM), streaming ASR with fewer parameters (78.2M Mamba beats 94.7M Causal Transformer)

Rigorous experimental methodology: Fair comparisons with identical training setups, multiple model scales, statistical significance testing (paired t-tests), and thoughtful ablations on bidirectional variants
Insightful representation analysis: Multi-scale phone purity analysis, CCA revealing speaker information capture, honest discussion of metric-performance discrepancies, provides design guidance
Well-executed and clear presentation: Strong organization, explicit implementation details, adherence to HuBERT pipeline, appropriate visualizations
weaknesses: Significant training setup deviation: Single GPU with 8× larger batch size and ~1/4 audio per batch compared to original HuBERT, confounding factor that undermines clean assessment of Mamba advantages and reproducibility

Scale-dependent and inconsistent bidirectional results: Base-size ExtBiMamba substantially underperforms Transformer on SUPERB (868.93 vs. 815.38), indicating scalability issues in the most generally applicable setting, limiting generality of claims

Unexplained discrepancy between representation metrics and downstream performance: ExtBiMamba has higher phone purity than Transformer yet worse phoneme recognition, suggesting phone purity is not valid quality metric; paper attributes to instability rather than providing concrete explanation
Limited dataset scope: Long-context ASR evaluated only on TEDLIUM3 (single domain); no multilingual evaluation despite SSL being multi-domain; generalization of advantages unclear
Modest novelty: Straightforward approach of replacing Transformer blocks with Mamba; no novel SSL procedures or architectural innovations; primarily empirical rather than methodological contribution

Incomplete mechanistic analysis: Shows Mamba excels in causal settings but doesn't deeply investigate why; limited guidance on when to use which variant; missing comparisons with other efficient Transformer variants

Reproducibility limitations: No code/model release mentioned; single GPU setup makes pre-training reproduction difficult; SUPERB evaluation concerns (only 4/13 tasks; authors cite SUPERB instability yet rely on it)
Incomplete computational analysis: MACs/RTF only on single GPU type; no memory consumption, power usage, or practical deployment (mobile/edge) implications discussed

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across multiple dimensions (computational efficiency, fine-tuning, representation analysis, SUPERB benchmarking) with extensive empirical analysis

Clear identification of practical advantages in specialized settings: significant improvements for long-context ASR (13.37% → 11.08% WER) and causal ASR (78.2M Mamba outperforms 94.7M Transformer at 15.77% vs 16.66% WER)
Strong reproducibility emphasis with detailed experimental specifications, code release, honest discussion of limitations, and controlled single-GPU setup for fair baseline comparisons

Novel empirical insights including discovery of training instability in ExtBiMamba, the finding that higher phone purity doesn't guarantee better downstream performance, and identification of scale-dependent architectural tradeoffs between ExtBiMamba and InnBiMamba
Rigorous layerwise representation analysis showing Mamba captures speaker-related features more distinctly (higher CCA similarity) and yields higher phone purity in quantized representations
Well-motivated exploration addressing gap in prior literature—most prior work evaluates Mamba on single tasks, while this provides unified cross-task evaluation
weaknesses: Significant scalability limitation undermines generalizability: all training on single V100 GPU with reduced batch sizes (~1/4 original), producing SUPERB scores substantially lower than official FAIR models; no scaling experiments to validate whether conclusions hold at larger scales, critical for foundation models

Bidirectional performance severely limits practical applicability: ExtBiMamba Base substantially underperforms Transformer Base (SUPERB_S 815.38 vs 868.93, PR 10.65% vs 7.49%; full SUPERB 683.59 vs 772.4); since bidirectional models are standard in practice, this is a major limitation

Unresolved training instability issues in ExtBiMamba (Appendix D shows persistent loss oscillations throughout training), suggesting architectural challenges rather than mere optimization issues, without proposed solutions
Limited novelty: primarily applies existing Mamba variants to speech SSL without architectural innovations or solutions to identified problems (stability, scalability)
Causal ASR advantage conflates model size with architecture (78.2M Mamba vs 94.7M Transformer); size-matched baseline needed for fair attribution
Disconnect between representation quality metrics and downstream performance: ExtBiMamba shows higher phone purity but worse PR probing results, somewhat undermining value of representation analysis

Practical advantages concentrated in narrow use cases (long-context documents, streaming ASR) while underperforming in standard bidirectional settings used in most real applications; long-context advantage partly due to Transformer OOM, which could be addressed with memory optimizations

Single training runs without multiple seeds or error bars; no mechanistic analysis of why Mamba captures speaker information differently; limited practical guidance for practitioners on architecture selection

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper provides a more systematic exploration than prior work, covering fine-tuning performance, representational analysis via phone purity and CCA, and SUPERB probing across multiple settings

Concrete computational efficiency gains: Clear demonstration of Mamba's advantages for long-context processing (linear vs quadratic scaling), with measured MACs/RTF and practical improvements (WER 13.37→11.08% on long-context ASR)
Reproducibility-focused design: Single-GPU training with released codebase enables reproduction, and authors transparently document experimental constraints

Valuable negative results and insights: Identifies training stability issues (Appendix D), scalability challenges in bidirectional settings, and the disconnect between phone purity and downstream performance—useful for practitioners
Thorough representation analysis: Layer-wise CCA analysis reveals that Mamba captures speaker information more distinctly and shows steeper phonetic feature progression
weaknesses: Very limited novelty: This is primarily an application paper combining existing HuBERT training with off-the-shelf Mamba blocks. No new architectures, methods, or theoretical insights are proposed. The contribution is largely 'we trained this combination and measured it.'

Fundamental scalability failure in practical bidirectional setting: ExtBiMamba Base scores 815.38 vs Transformer Base 868.93 on SUPERB (53-point gap). Full SUPERB shows 683.5 vs 772.4. These are substantial performance drops in the setting most applicable to real-world use cases

Training instability undermines core advantages: Figure 7 shows ExtBiMamba exhibits persistent loss-scale oscillations throughout training, contradicting Mamba's appeal as a stable alternative. Authors acknowledge this may require 'hybrid blocks' or 'attention mechanisms'—which defeats the purpose of using Mamba

Confounded experimental design limiting validity: (i) Single GPU training uses 1/4 batch size of original HuBERT, acknowledged to reduce SUPERB scores below published baselines, making comparisons unreliable; (ii) Single training run per configuration without averaging; (iii) Streaming ASR compares 78M vs 94M parameter models—architecture differences are confounded with parameter count

Mixed and inconsistent results across settings: Causal setting advantages are modest (~1-2% on phone recognition, 0.89% WER improvement on streaming). Results are setting-dependent and don't support universal advantages. Only small-scale models show bidirectional competitiveness

Unresolved disconnect between analyses: Phone purity shows ExtBiMamba superiority (Figure 2), yet SUPERB phoneme recognition shows Transformer advantage (7.49% vs 10.65% PER). Authors acknowledge this but provide no satisfying explanation, raising questions about the interpretability of the representation analysis

Long-context ASR comparison is not entirely fair: Transformer baseline reaches OOM—expected for quadratic complexity. This is a known architectural limitation, not evidence that Mamba is a superior alternative for contexts where Transformer cannot run

Limited evaluation scope: Only 2 detailed fine-tuning tasks (long-context, causal ASR). SUPERB evaluation uses only 4 of 10 tasks. No evaluation on other important applications (generation, machine translation, etc.). This is narrow for drawing broad conclusions

Overstated contributions in abstract/introduction: Claims of 'superior performance' and 'promising complementary direction' are not supported by full results. The bidirectional setting—most practical—shows clear Transformer superiority at scale

Relevant for speech venues, not general NLP: This is primarily an empirical study applying existing methods to a domain-specific problem. Better suited for Interspeech/ASRU where speech-specific contributions are more valued than ACL

strengths: First comprehensive cross-task evaluation of Mamba-based speech SSL models, addressing a clear gap in prior work limited to isolated tasks

Rigorous computational efficiency analysis (MACs, RTF) with quantitative validation that Mamba maintains linear scaling while Transformers suffer quadratic growth, with empirical evidence of OOM errors beyond 80 seconds

Practical demonstrations of genuine utility: long-context ASR achieving 11.08% WER at document level (vs. OOM for Transformer), and streaming ASR with Mamba Base (78M params) outperforming larger Causal Transformer (94.7M) at 15.77% vs. 16.66% WER
Multi-perspective representation analysis including phone purity across layers and CCA analysis with multiple attributes (phoneme, speaker, emotion), providing insights beyond benchmark numbers
Methodological rigor with controlled comparisons, statistical significance testing (paired t-tests), ablation studies, and fair baseline setup

Strong transparency and reproducibility emphasis: honest limitations section, training dynamics analysis explaining instability, promised code release, and single-GPU setup enabling reproducibility despite lower absolute scale
Clear and well-presented paper with effective visualizations (Figure 1 clearly shows efficiency trade-offs) and comprehensive tables
weaknesses: Significant bidirectional scalability limitation: ExtBiMamba Base (94.3M) substantially underperforms Transformer Base (94.7M) with PR of 10.65% vs. 7.49% (42% relative error increase) and SUPERB_S of 815.38 vs. 868.93, limiting practical applicability for most downstream tasks
Training conducted on single GPU with batch size ~1/4 of original HuBERT setup, resulting in lower absolute performance and reduced generalizability; no averaging across multiple training runs

Mixed downstream results on standard SUPERB benchmarks: superior in causal settings but underperforming in bidirectional settings at base scale, limiting ability to recommend Mamba as a general alternative to Transformers

Disconnect between representation quality metrics and downstream performance: ExtBiMamba exhibits higher phone purity (Section 5.1) but underperforms on PR probing (Section 6.2), raising questions about metric utility
Training instability in ExtBiMamba (Appendix D) with persistent loss scale oscillations throughout training, suggesting potential reliability concerns for production deployment
Limited long-context ASR comparison: only Mamba evaluated at document level due to Transformer OOM, no direct comparison with memory-efficient Transformer variants for fair evaluation
Primarily empirical contribution using existing architectures (ExtBiMamba/InnBiMamba from prior work) and standard HuBERT training without methodological innovations
Incomplete downstream evaluation using only 4 of 10 SUPERB tasks, with full evaluation relegated to appendix; Table 6 reveals performance gaps on semantic and emotion tasks
Shallow mechanistic explanation for Mamba's causal superiority—descriptive rather than explanatory, lacking deep insights into why State Space Models excel in this domain
CCA analysis finding that Mamba maintains higher speaker similarity lacks mechanistic explanation; hyperparameter choices (different learning rates for different model sizes) not fully justified
